analogy.p: Think of the height of a ball thrown from a cliff edge, modelled by a quadratic. Solving the quadratic equal to 0 asks 'when is the height exactly at ground level?', and the two roots are the times when the curved path crosses the ground line. The completed-square form (x + p)² + q tells you the highest (or lowest) point and when it happens, like the peak of the ball's flight. It breaks down because a real ball only exists for positive times, whereas the algebra gives two solutions and one is often negative and must be rejected.
analogy.t: A ball thrown upwards and the ground

bullets: **Standard form** is ax² + bx + c = 0: **a** is the coefficient of x², **b** the coefficient of x, **c** the constant term.
If a = 0 the x² term disappears and the equation is **linear**, not quadratic.
The solutions are the values of x that make the left-hand side equal to **zero**; substitute them back to check.
A quadratic has **at most two** real solutions, so if you find three you have made an error.
The roots are the **x-intercepts** of the graph y = ax² + bx + c, linking algebra to graphs.
Higher-tier questions often say **'give your answer to 3 significant figures'** or **'give your answer in the form p ± √q'**, which is a signal that factorising will not work.
Questions that say 'solve by factorising' require **factorising**, and an answer from the formula alone will not gain full marks.
core.p: A **quadratic equation** is an equation that can be written in the form **ax² + bx + c = 0**, where a, b and c are numbers and **a is not zero**. The highest power of x is 2, which is why the graph is a **parabola** (a U-shaped curve). The specification asks you to solve quadratic equations (with integer coefficients) **by factorising, by using the quadratic formula and by completing the square**, and to give answers in surd form or rounded when asked. A quadratic can have **two solutions, one repeated solution, or no real solutions**, because the curve y = ax² + bx + c can cross the x-axis twice, touch it once, or miss it. The solutions are also called **roots**, and they are the x-values where the graph meets the x-axis.

bullets: **Zero product rule**: if A × B = 0 then A = 0 or B = 0 (or both).
x² = 5x − 6 → **x² − 5x + 6 = 0**; subtract 5x and add 6 to both sides.
(x − 3)(x + 2) = 6 is **not** solved by x − 3 = 6; expand to x² − x − 6 = 6, then x² − x − 12 = 0.
It is usually neatest to keep the **x² coefficient positive**; if it is negative, multiply every term by −1.
**Never divide both sides by x** (for example x² = 4x → x = 4), as you lose the solution x = 0; instead write x² − 4x = 0 → x(x − 4) = 0.
If there are fractions, multiply through by the common denominator before rearranging.
core.h: Step one every time: get the equation equal to zero
core.p: Almost all methods for solving quadratics rely on the equation being **equal to 0**, because of the **zero product rule**: if two numbers multiply to give 0, at least one of them must be 0. Before you do anything else, **move every term to one side** so that the other side is 0, and collect like terms into ax² + bx + c = 0. For instance, x² = 5x − 6 becomes x² − 5x + 6 = 0, and x(x + 2) = 15 becomes x² + 2x − 15 = 0 after expanding the bracket. A very common mistake is to solve something like (x − 3)(x + 2) = 6 by setting each bracket to 6; this is wrong because the product must be **zero** for the rule to apply.

bullets: x² − 5x − 14 = 0: pairs of 14 are 1×14 and 2×7; c is negative so the signs differ; the pair that adds to −5 is **−7 and +2**, giving (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0, so **x = 7 or x = −2**.
x² + 7x + 12 = 0: numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7 are 3 and 4, giving (x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, so **x = −3 or x = −4**.
x² − 8x + 15 = 0: both numbers negative (c positive, b negative): −3 and −5, so **x = 3 or x = 5**.
**Be careful with signs of the solutions**: (x − 7) = 0 gives x = +7, and (x + 2) = 0 gives x = −2.
**Check** by expanding the brackets: (x − 7)(x + 2) = x² + 2x − 7x − 14 = x² − 5x − 14 ✓.
Also check by substituting: 7² − 5×7 − 14 = 49 − 35 − 14 = 0 ✓.
Write the line (x − 7)(x + 2) = 0 clearly; the mark scheme gives a method mark for the correct brackets.
core.p: When a = 1 the equation is x² + bx + c = 0. You look for **two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b**; call them p and q. Then the quadratic factorises as **(x + p)(x + q) = 0**, and by the zero product rule x = −p or x = −q. The signs of the numbers follow the signs of b and c: if c is **positive** the two numbers have the **same sign** (both positive if b is positive, both negative if b is negative); if c is **negative** the numbers have **different signs** and the larger one takes the sign of b. List the factor pairs of c systematically so that you do not miss one.

bullets: Step 1: multiply **a × c**; Step 2: find a pair with product ac and sum b; Step 3: **split** the bx term; Step 4: factorise in **pairs**; Step 5: take out the common **bracket**.
Solutions: 3x − 1 = 0 gives **x = 1/3**; x + 2 = 0 gives **x = −2**.
Check by expanding: (3x − 1)(x + 2) = 3x² + 6x − x − 2 = 3x² + 5x − 2 ✓.
If the two pairs do not give a common bracket you have mis-signed a term; take out a **minus sign** when necessary, as in −1(x + 2).
If no pair of numbers works for ac and b, the quadratic **does not factorise**, so use the formula.
Where a common factor exists (for example 6x² + 10x − 4 = 2(3x² + 5x − 2)), take it out **first** to make the numbers smaller.
core.h: Solving by factorising when a is greater than 1 (Higher)
core.p: When a is not 1, for example 3x² + 5x − 2 = 0, the quickest reliable method is the **ac method**. Multiply a by c (3 × −2 = −6), find two numbers that multiply to give **ac** and add to give **b** (here **6 and −1**, since 6 × −1 = −6 and 6 + (−1) = 5), then **split the middle term** using those numbers: 3x² + 6x − x − 2 = 0. Factorise the first two terms and the last two terms to get 3x(x + 2) − 1(x + 2) = 0, and the common bracket gives **(3x − 1)(x + 2) = 0**. The solutions are x = 1/3 and x = −2. Alternatively you can use trial and improvement on the brackets, but the ac method never fails if the quadratic does factorise.

bullets: x² − 4x = 0 → x(x − 4) = 0 → **x = 0 or x = 4**; never divide by x.
x² + 6x + 9 = 0 → (x + 3)² = 0 → **x = −3** (a repeated root; the curve touches the x-axis).
A **sum** of two squares such as x² + 9 does **not** factorise and x² + 9 = 0 has **no real solutions**.
Spot these first: no middle term suggests difference of two squares or x² = number; no constant suggests a common factor of x.
core.h: Special cases: difference of two squares, no constant term, perfect squares
core.p: Three special types are quick to spot and worth knowing. A **difference of two squares** has the form x² − k² and factorises as **(x − k)(x + k)**, so x² − 49 = 0 gives x = 7 or x = −7. A quadratic with **no constant term**, such as x² − 4x = 0, factorises by taking out a **common factor x** to give x(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4. A **perfect square** like x² + 6x + 9 factorises as (x + 3)², and the solution x = −3 appears twice, which is called a **repeated root** (the graph just touches the x-axis). Recognising these saves time and reduces the chance of error in a non-calculator paper.

bullets: **x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a**: learn it word for word; a common rhyme or tune helps.
Write down **a = …, b = …, c = …** with their signs before substituting.
If b is negative, −b is positive: for b = −3, −b = **+3**, and b² = (−3)² = **9** (not −9).
Calculate **b² − 4ac** separately first (this part is called the **discriminant**); if c or a is negative, −4ac becomes **positive**.
The line 2a is the **whole denominator**, so divide the entire numerator by it, not just the root.
On a calculator write the answer as **two separate calculations** (+ then −) and store the root to avoid rounding early.
Give answers to the accuracy requested (for example **3 significant figures** or 2 decimal places), and show an unrounded form or more figures first to earn the method mark.
core.p: When a quadratic will not factorise, or when the question asks for decimal or surd answers, use the **quadratic formula**. For ax² + bx + c = 0, the solutions are **x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a**. The formula is **not given** on the Edexcel formulae sheet, so it must be learnt. The ± symbol means you calculate **two** answers, one using + and one using −. You must first make sure the equation is in the form ax² + bx + c = 0, then identify a, b and c **with their signs**, then substitute into the formula using **brackets** around negative numbers. The whole of the top line, including −b, is divided by 2a, and the square root covers the whole of b² − 4ac only.

bullets: **b² − 4ac > 0**: two distinct real roots; the graph crosses the x-axis **twice**.
**b² − 4ac = 0**: one repeated root x = −b/(2a); the graph **touches** the x-axis.
**b² − 4ac < 0**: **no real roots**; the graph does not reach the x-axis.
x² + 2x + 5 = 0: b² − 4ac = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0, so there are **no real solutions**.
Leaving the answer in **surd form** gives an exact value, for example x = (3 ± √41)/4, which is accepted when the question asks for exact answers.
If the discriminant is a **perfect square** (like 49), the quadratic factorises, a useful check on whether factorising was possible.
core.h: Using the formula: a full example and the discriminant
core.p: Take 2x² − 3x − 4 = 0, so a = 2, b = −3, c = −4. The discriminant is b² − 4ac = (−3)² − 4 × 2 × (−4) = 9 + 32 = 41. Then x = (3 ± √41)/4, which gives x = (3 + 6.403…)/4 = 2.35 and x = (3 − 6.403…)/4 = −0.851 to 3 significant figures. The **discriminant** b² − 4ac tells you how many solutions there are before you finish: if it is **positive** there are two different real solutions, if it is **zero** there is one repeated solution, and if it is **negative** you cannot take the square root so there are **no real solutions**. A calculator will show a maths error for the negative case, which is a useful warning that the equation has no real roots.

bullets: x² + 6x − 2: half of 6 is 3, so (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9; subtract 9 to correct it: **(x + 3)² − 9 − 2 = (x + 3)² − 11**.
x² + 5x + 1 = (x + 5/2)² − 25/4 + 1 = **(x + 5/2)² − 21/4** (halves can be fractions).
Always **expand your answer back out** to check you get the original expression.
The completed-square form (x + p)² + q gives the **turning point (−p, q)** of the graph, linking to graph topics.
core.p: **Completing the square** rewrites x² + bx + c in the form **(x + p)² + q**, where **p = b/2** and **q = c − p²**. The idea comes from geometry: x² + 6x is a square of side x plus two rectangles of 3 by x, and you need an extra 3 × 3 square to complete a bigger square of side (x + 3). That is why you add and subtract **(b/2)²**. So x² + 6x − 2 = (x + 3)² − 9 − 2 = **(x + 3)² − 11**, and x² − 8x + 3 = **(x − 4)² − 13**. Note that the sign inside the bracket is the **same as the sign of b**, and you must **halve** b, never double it. When a is not 1, take a out of the x² and x terms first: 2x² + 12x + 5 = 2(x² + 6x) + 5 = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] + 5 = **2(x + 3)² − 13**.

bullets: If the right-hand side of (x + p)² = k is **negative**, there are **no real solutions**, since a square cannot be negative.
The answer **x = −3 ± √11** is the exact form; give it when the question asks for exact answers or 'in surd form'.
This method **always works**, even when the quadratic does not factorise; the formula is derived from it.
A good check: the two solutions are **symmetric** about x = −p (here −3), since they differ by ±√11.
Be careful with fractions: x² + 5x + 1 = 0 → (x + 5/2)² = 21/4 → x = −5/2 ± √21/2.
core.h: Solving a quadratic by completing the square
core.p: Once the quadratic is in completed-square form you can solve it by **undoing the operations**: x² + 6x − 2 = 0 becomes (x + 3)² − 11 = 0, so (x + 3)² = 11, then x + 3 = ±√11, so **x = −3 ± √11**. Numerically √11 = 3.3166…, which gives x = 0.317 and x = −6.32 to 3 significant figures. This method is used when the question says **'solve by completing the square'**, and it gives exact surd answers directly. For a ≠ 1, divide through by a after completing the square: 2x² + 12x + 5 = 0 becomes 2(x + 3)² − 13 = 0, so (x + 3)² = 13/2, and x = −3 ± √(13/2). Do not forget the ± when you take the square root, which is the most common lost mark.

bullets: Try **factorising** first when the numbers are small and the question does not ask for decimals.
Use the **formula** when asked for answers to a given number of significant figures or decimal places.
Use **completing the square** when told to, or when the answer must be in the form p ± √q.
If b = 0 (for example x² = 20), simply **square root both sides**: x = ±√20 = ±2√5.
If c = 0 (no constant term), **factorise by taking out x**.
In a **'show that'** question, show the quadratic form and a method, not just a calculator value.
If a question provides a **graph** and asks for solutions, read off the x-intercepts.
core.p: Method choice saves time and avoids mistakes. If the question tells you the method, you **must use it** to earn full marks. If it does not, look for clues: **whole-number solutions** or the instruction 'solve' with small coefficients suggest **factorising**; **'give your answer to 3 significant figures'** or 'to 2 decimal places' means the quadratic probably does not factorise, so use the **formula**; **'give your answer in the form p ± √q'** or 'by completing the square' calls for completing the square. On a calculator paper you may use the calculator's equation solver to **check** answers, but you must still show working. If factorising does not work after about a minute, move to the formula.

bullets: **Form** the equation: write the area, perimeter or Pythagoras relation using the given algebraic lengths.
**Expand** the brackets and **collect** all terms on one side to give ax² + bx + c = 0.
**Solve** by the most suitable method, then **substitute** back into the lengths to check.
**Reject** invalid solutions with a reason, such as 'length cannot be negative'.
Consecutive integers n and n + 1 with product 90: n(n + 1) = 90 → n² + n − 90 = 0 → (n + 10)(n − 9) = 0 → **n = 9** (positive integers), numbers 9 and 10.
Pythagoras: sides x, x + 1 and hypotenuse 5: x² + (x + 1)² = 25 → 2x² + 2x − 24 = 0 → x² + x − 12 = 0 → (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0 → **x = 3**.
Give the **final answer in context** with units, such as 'width = 5 cm'.
core.h: Forming and solving quadratics from problems
core.p: Many exam questions are set in context: areas of rectangles, Pythagoras, consecutive numbers or ages. You must first **form** the equation from the information, expand and rearrange it to ax² + bx + c = 0, then solve it, and finally **interpret** the answer. Interpretation matters: lengths and times cannot be negative, so one of the solutions is often **rejected** with a short reason. For example, a rectangle has length (x + 3) cm and width (x − 1) cm and area 45 cm². Then (x + 3)(x − 1) = 45, so x² + 2x − 3 = 45, so x² + 2x − 48 = 0, so (x + 8)(x − 6) = 0, giving x = −8 or x = 6. Since a length cannot be negative, **x = 6**, so the rectangle is 9 cm by 5 cm (area 45 ✓).

bullets: Multiply **every term** (including those not in fractions) by the common denominator.
3/x + 2 = x → 3 + 2x = x² → x² − 2x − 3 = 0 → **x = 3 or x = −1**; both valid.
Simultaneous: y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25 → x² + (x + 1)² = 25 → 2x² + 2x − 24 = 0 → x² + x − 12 = 0 → x = 3 or −4 (find y after).
Equations with **x⁴** such as x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 become quadratics in x² (let u = x²), which is rare but good practice.
After solving, check no **denominator** becomes zero.
The quadratic formula also works if the coefficients are **fractions or decimals**, but clearing fractions first is neater.
Always return to the **original equation** to check that the solutions fit.
core.p: Some equations do not look quadratic but become quadratic after rearranging. **Algebraic fractions** are the commonest: to solve 3/x + 2 = x, multiply every term by x to get 3 + 2x = x², rearrange to **x² − 2x − 3 = 0**, factorise as (x − 3)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1. Check in the original: 3/3 + 2 = 3 ✓ and 3/(−1) + 2 = −1 ✓. Another case is **simultaneous equations** where one is linear and one is a circle or curve; substituting the linear into the other gives a quadratic in one letter. Whenever you clear denominators, check that no solution makes a denominator **zero**, since such a solution is invalid.

bullets: **Roots** are the x-intercepts: where y = 0.
The **line of symmetry** is x = −b/(2a), halfway between the roots.
The **turning point** lies on the line of symmetry; here x = 0.5 gives y = 0.25 − 0.5 − 6 = **−6.25**.
The **sum of the roots** is −b/a (here 1) and the **product** is c/a (here −6), a useful check.
To solve x² − x − 6 = 4, draw **y = 4** and read the intersections.
If the curve does not cross the x-axis the equation has **no real solutions**.
A positive x² coefficient gives a **U shape** (minimum); a negative one gives an **∩ shape** (maximum).
core.h: Solving quadratics from graphs and symmetry
core.p: The solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0 are the **x-coordinates where the graph of y = ax² + bx + c crosses the x-axis**. For y = x² − x − 6, the graph crosses at x = −2 and x = 3, which are the roots of x² − x − 6 = 0. The graph is **symmetrical** about a vertical line through the turning point, so the line of symmetry is halfway between the roots: x = (−2 + 3)/2 = **0.5**, which equals **−b/(2a)**. To solve an equation like x² − x − 6 = 4 from the same graph, draw the line y = 4 and read the x-values where it meets the curve. Graphical solutions are usually only accurate to the scale of the graph, so give them to 1 decimal place unless told otherwise.

bullets: **Turning points**: (x + p)² + q has minimum point **(−p, q)**.
**Simultaneous equations**: linear + quadratic or circle leads to a quadratic to solve.
**Algebraic fractions**: clearing denominators often leaves a quadratic.
**Trigonometry**: solving 2sin²x = sin x style equations by factorising.
**Algebraic proof**: showing that an expression like n² + n is always even uses factorising.
**Projectiles in science**: s = ut + ½at² is a quadratic in t.
**Iteration**: x² − 3x − 1 = 0 can be rearranged as x = 3 + 1/x or x = √(3x + 1).
core.p: Quadratic equations connect to many other parts of the specification. In **graphs**, the completed-square form gives the turning point, and the roots give the intercepts. In **algebraic fractions** and **proof**, quadratics arise when you simplify or equate expressions. In **simultaneous equations** with a non-linear equation, substitution gives a quadratic. In **geometry and trigonometry**, Pythagoras and area problems often produce quadratics, and equations such as sin²x = 1/4 are solved like quadratics. **Iteration** also uses rearrangement of quadratic equations to find approximate roots, and in **sequences** the nth term of a quadratic sequence is a quadratic expression.

bullets: **Rearrange to = 0** first and write the standard form on its own line.
For factorising, write the **brackets**, then each **x = …** answer on separate lines.
For the formula, write **a, b, c**, the substituted formula with brackets, then both answers.
Give **both solutions** unless the context rejects one; if you reject, say why.
Do not round until the **end**; use the calculator's stored values.
Round as the question requires: **3 s.f.** or **2 d.p.**, and state exact form first if you can.
Check by **substituting** one answer into the original equation if time allows.
For 'solve by completing the square', **start** with (x + p)² + q; going straight to the formula loses method marks.
core.p: Quadratic questions typically carry 3 marks for factorising, 3 or 4 marks for the formula or completing the square, and 4 or 5 marks in context. The mark scheme awards **M1** for correct factorisation or a correct substitution, **M1** for correct solving of brackets or evaluation of the root, and **A1** for both correct solutions. Show the equation set to zero, show the brackets or the substituted formula, then give both answers clearly. Lost marks usually come from sign errors, missing solutions, rounding too early, and not meeting the instruction (such as using the formula when told to factorise).

exam: **'Solve'** with small whole-number coefficients usually expects **factorising**; always write the brackets and then each solution.
If the question says **'give your answer to 3 significant figures'**, use the **quadratic formula**; the method marks come from correct substitution.
**'Solve by completing the square'** needs the completed-square form (x + p)² + q shown before the solutions.
**'Give your answer in the form p ± √q'** is a strong clue to complete the square, or to use the formula and simplify.
Typical marks: **3 marks** factorise and solve (M1 brackets, M1 each x = …, A1); **3 marks** formula (M1 substitution, M1 evaluation, A1 both answers).
In a context question (**4 to 5 marks**), the marks are for forming the equation, rearranging to zero, solving, and **rejecting or choosing** the valid answer.
Write **a, b, c** and the substituted formula with **brackets** around negatives; a sign error in b² or −b is the most common lost mark.
**Rearrange to zero first**; never solve (x − 3)(x + 2) = 6 by setting each bracket equal to 6.
Check your **solutions** by substituting back into the original equation, even briefly.
On a calculator paper, use the equation-solver to **check**, but show full working because answers alone often earn 0 or 1 mark.
For graph-based questions, read off the **x-intercepts** for y = 0, or intersections with a horizontal line for equations equal to a number.

mistakes.r: Rearrange to = 0 first: x² − 5x + 6 = 0; the zero product rule only works for a product equal to 0.
mistakes.w: Solving x² = 5x − 6 without setting it to zero, or setting (x − 3)(x + 2) = 6 to x − 3 = 6

mistakes.r: Reverse the sign: x − 7 = 0 gives x = 7 and x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2.
Write x² − 4x = 0 → x(x − 4) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 4; dividing by x loses the solution x = 0.
Calculate two answers using + and −, and divide the whole numerator by 2a.
mistakes.w: Giving only the + answer from the formula, or putting the ± inside only part of the formula

mistakes.r: The root covers all of b² − 4ac, and the 2a divides the entire numerator.
mistakes.w: Taking the square root of only part of b² − 4ac, or dividing only the root by 2a

mistakes.r: Halve b to get (x + 3)², then subtract 3² = 9 to balance: (x + 3)² − 9.
mistakes.w: Completing the square: (x + 6)² for x² + 6x, or forgetting to subtract the extra 9

mistakes.r: x + 3 = ±√11, so x = −3 ± √11; there are two solutions.
Keep full calculator values until the end and round to the accuracy requested (3 s.f. or 2 d.p.).
mistakes.w: Rounding midway or giving answers to the wrong accuracy

mistakes.r: Reject solutions that do not fit the context and state the reason, such as 'length cannot be negative'.
mistakes.w: Leaving a negative length or a time as an answer

summary: You must be able to solve quadratic equations with integer coefficients by factorising, by the quadratic formula and by completing the square, rearranging to equal zero first, giving exact or rounded answers as asked, and rejecting solutions that do not fit a context. This is one of the most heavily examined Higher algebra skills, appearing in graphs, problems and proofs.

svg.cap: The graph of y = x² − x − 6 crosses the x-axis at the two roots, x = −2 and x = 3, with its minimum on the line of symmetry x = 0.5.
Choosing a method: rearrange to zero, then factorise if possible, otherwise use the formula or complete the square.

terms.d: An equation that can be written as ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0.
The number multiplying a variable in a term, for example 3 in 3x².
The term with no variable in it, c in ax² + bx + c.
A value of x that makes the equation true; for a quadratic, an x-intercept of the graph.
The form ax² + bx + c = 0, with every term on one side.
Write an expression as a product of brackets, such as x² − 5x − 14 = (x − 7)(x + 2).
If the product of two factors is zero then at least one of the factors is zero.
An expression of the form a² − b², which factorises as (a − b)(a + b).
An expression that is a bracket squared, such as x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)².
A solution that occurs twice, so the graph touches the x-axis without crossing it.
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, which gives the solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0.
The expression b² − 4ac; its sign tells you the number of real roots.
Rewriting x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.
An irrational root left in exact form, such as √11.
The U-shaped or ∩-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic.
The minimum or maximum point of a parabola; for (x + p)² + q it is (−p, q).
The vertical line through the turning point of a parabola, x = −b/(2a).
Digits counted from the first non-zero digit, used to round answers to a given accuracy.

worked.q: (a) Write x² + 6x − 2 in the form (x + p)² + q. (b) Hence solve x² + 6x − 2 = 0, giving your answers to 3 significant figures. (4 marks)
steps: Half of 6 is 3, so p = 3; (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9 (M1).
